{{Update|date=July 2025}}

In [[queueing theory]], an '''adversarial queueing network''' is a model where the traffic to the network is supplied by an [[adversary model|opponent]] rather than as the result of a [[stochastic process]].

==History==
The model was first introduced in 1996.<ref>{{Cite book | doi = 10.1145/237814.237984| chapter = Adversarial queueing theory| title = Proceedings of the twenty-eighth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing – STOC '96| pages = 376| year = 1996| last1 = Borodin | first1 = A. | authorlink1 = Allan Borodin| last2 = Kleinberg | first2 = J. | authorlink2 = Jon Kleinberg| last3 = Raghavan | first3 = P. | authorlink3 = Prabhakar Raghavan| last4 = Sudan | first4 = M. | authorlink4 = Madhu Sudan| last5 = Williamson | first5 = D. P. | authorlink5 = David P. Williamson| isbn = 0897917855| s2cid = 771941}}</ref> It has seen use in describing the impact of [[packet injection]]s on the performance of [[communication networks]].<ref>{{Cite book | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-45198-3_14| chapter = Effective Routing and Scheduling in Adversarial Queueing Networks| title = Approximation, Randomization, and Combinatorial Optimization.. Algorithms and Techniques| volume = 2764| pages = 153| series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science| year = 2003| last1 = Sethuraman | first1 = J. | last2 = Teo | first2 = C. P. | isbn = 978-3-540-40770-6| url = http://www.columbia.edu/~js1353/pubs/st-adversarial.pdf}}</ref> The stability of an adversarial queueing network can be determined by considering a [[fluid limit]].<ref>{{Cite book | doi = 10.1109/SFCS.1998.743429| chapter = Stability of adversarial queues via fluid models| title = Proceedings 39th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (Cat. No.98CB36280)| pages = 60–70| year = 1998| last1 = Gamarnik | first1 = D.|author1-link=David Gamarnik |isbn = 0-8186-9172-7| s2cid = 2145524}}</ref>
